title: One-time in vivo correction of severe newborn metabolic disease before irreversible injury

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a reusable treatment platform that corrects a disease-causing genetic defect inside an infant’s liver early enough to prevent irreversible metabolic injury. A single administration would restore enough function in hepatocytes—the liver cells responsible for many metabolic reactions—to control the disease durably and reduce or eliminate burdensome lifelong treatment. The strongest scope is severe inherited metabolic disease in which restoring sufficient hepatic enzyme activity can prevent systemic accumulation of toxic substances.

The platform would combine rapid diagnosis, variant-specific editor design, manufacturing, safety assessment, regulatory review and early clinical delivery. Its defining advance would be the ability to move from one successfully treated child to additional genes and variants through a substantially abbreviated development pathway. An individualized treatment establishes an important component; a reusable preventive platform also requires evidence that treatment can arrive within the relevant disease window and work consistently across more than one genetic target. The October 2025 meeting account describes this transition as a development goal.

significance.text: Severe metabolic disease can be diagnosed early yet still cause neurologic injury and require demanding chronic care. For MMUT-deficient methylmalonic acidemia, the reviewed article describes diagnosis in the first days to weeks of life, neurologic risk and lifelong dietary protein restriction. If a single early treatment could safely provide sustained metabolic control, early diagnosis could lead directly to prevention of otherwise avoidable injury and reduced treatment dependence. Prevention of death, preservation of development and relief of family treatment burden would be consequential clinical benefits to establish.

The broader enabling advance would be repeatability across rare variants. A shared development framework could make individualized correction feasible for children whose mutations would otherwise require separate development efforts. The proposed master protocol described in October 2025 offers a concrete pathway toward this goal through gene-specific investigational applications and variant-specific amendments. The supplied evidence does not establish how much time or cost such a pathway would save, or support a universal decade-long development baseline for each variant.

Restoring liver function would not automatically ensure typical development or prevent every complication. Methylmalonic acidemia affects multiple organs, including the central nervous system, kidneys and heart, so extrahepatic disease may persist despite hepatic improvement. Preventing metabolically mediated brain injury remains a plausible conditional benefit in suitable disorders, but it must be demonstrated. Extending this concept to diseases requiring correction within the brain would require additional delivery capabilities; success in liver-directed treatment would not establish that extension.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability is the integration of safe, sufficiently effective hepatic correction with delivery before irreversible injury. Editing a measurable fraction of cells is an intermediate result: the clinically relevant requirement is enough restored metabolic function to prevent crises and sustain control under normal growth, feeding and illness. The MMA study illustrates why evidence suggesting an editing mechanism cannot substitute for clinical efficacy, while the personalized CPS1 experience illustrates feasibility without establishing prevention of neonatal injury.

Engineering synthesis: the treatment pathway must fit inside a disease-specific window for preventing injury. This requires prompt molecular diagnosis, selection of an appropriate correction strategy, reliable manufacture and release, and treatment while the infant remains eligible for prevention. A one-time treatment must also deliver sufficient functional correction durably as the child grows. Safety assessment must address unintended editing, delivery-related toxicity and delayed harms as well as the intended metabolic benefit. The supplied record does not establish the required editing fraction, minimum functional restoration or manufacturing turnaround for each disease.

Platform reuse also requires a defensible boundary between what can be shared and what must be tested anew. The October 2025 plan describes gene-specific INDs and amendments supported by in vitro evidence for each variant-specific guide RNA. It does not establish that retaining the same editor and lipid nanoparticle makes every new guide equivalent in safety, or that regulators have accepted omission of new animal toxicology for every variant. Establishing when prior manufacturing and toxicology evidence can be reused is part of the proposed breakthrough.

current_state.text: An October 7, 2025 GEN meeting account describes personalized lipid-nanoparticle base editing for an infant with carbamoyl-phosphate synthetase 1 deficiency. Treatment began at seven months of age, followed by escalating doses 22 and 62 days later. The account reports partial urea-cycle function and characterizes the intervention as clinical care rather than a clinical trial. This supports individualized human treatment feasibility. Three administrations do not demonstrate the proposed single-administration capability, and treatment starting at seven months does not establish prevention of neonatal injury. The supplied evidence also does not establish that this age was necessarily beyond the highest-risk period.

The research notes cite Musunuru, Ahrens-Nicklas and colleagues in the New England Journal of Medicine, dated May 15, 2025, DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2504747. They attribute to that paper infusions at about seven and eight months, increased dietary protein and reduced scavenger dosing over seven weeks, no serious adverse events during that interval, and a single-patient expanded-access designation. No text from that paper was retained for the supplied review, so these details remain attributed reports that could not be independently assessed there. The later meeting account’s third dose could extend an earlier two-dose report without contradicting it. Neither account, as available here, establishes unrestricted diet, freedom from medication or durable prevention of injury.

Bedoyan and colleagues reported the first-in-human phase 1/2 SUNRISE study of AAV-delivered, nuclease-free editing for MMUT-deficient methylmalonic acidemia in Gene Therapy on March 30, 2026, DOI 10.1038/s41434-026-00609-1. It involved four children aged 20–114 months, with a data cutoff of May 23, 2023; the publication date should not be read as the treatment date. Enrollment was terminated for lack of clinical efficacy. Integration was inferred from the circulating ALB-2A surrogate biomarker rather than directly confirmed in liver tissue, and serious treatment-related toxicities included thrombotic microangiopathy. The reviewed full main article supports these findings; supplementary material and figure images were not inspected.

The MMA investigators questioned whether liver-targeted nuclease-free editing would ultimately provide an effective treatment for MMA and called for additional investigation. That conclusion concerns the evaluated approach and disease; it does not establish that every nuclease-free strategy must fail. The study also differs materially from lipid-nanoparticle base editing in the CPS1 case. Together, these experiences show that delivery, mechanism, disease biology, clinical benefit and safety must be evaluated separately.

The October 2025 meeting account describes a planned master protocol spanning seven urea-cycle disorders, with gene-specific INDs and variant-specific guide amendments supported by in vitro data. It reports an intended development pathway, not a completed platform trial or demonstrated regulatory reuse. The supplied record therefore contains individualized treatment, a terminated pediatric editing study and a platform plan, without demonstrating the proposed preventive newborn platform. Its availability or trial status as of November 1, 2026 remains unverified because no freshness search was included in the supplied review.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed clinical demonstration: under one master protocol, infants with severe disease involving at least two different hepatic metabolic genes would receive a single administration before irreversible injury. Eligibility would require a disease-specific prespecified age window and, where applicable, treatment before any hyperammonemic crisis; absence of a recorded crisis alone would not establish absence of prior injury. For at least two years, participants would remain free of disease-specific metabolic crises, discontinue nitrogen-scavenger drugs where applicable, tolerate age-appropriate protein intake without therapeutic restriction, and meet prespecified developmental endpoints. These are proposed thresholds, not established standards or reported outcomes.
completion_criteria.label: Preinjury single-dose treatment across two genes meets two-year clinical endpoints

completion_criteria.text: Proposed evidence and safety requirements: metabolic benefit should be sustained across feeding, growth and ordinary intercurrent illness, with documented supportive care and a prespecified basis for interpreting outcomes against each disease’s expected course. The demonstration should exclude treatment-related liver failure and other serious treatment-related toxicity, rather than assessing liver failure alone. Longer surveillance would evaluate durability and delayed harms. Developmental assessment should distinguish prevention of new metabolic injury from persistent extrahepatic disease or injury that preceded treatment.
completion_criteria.label: Sustained metabolic benefit without serious treatment-related toxicity during follow-up

completion_criteria.text: Proposed platform demonstration: additional variants would be introduced by amendment using the same editor backbone and lipid nanoparticle, with variant-specific laboratory evidence and a justified, regulator-accepted approach to reusing relevant toxicology data. Independent manufacturing batches and treatment of multiple infants should show reproducible product quality and clinical benefit. The demonstration should document turnaround sufficiently short for the target disease window. Success across two genes, additional variants and two years of follow-up would establish a defined breadth of performance; it would not prove lifelong durability or applicability to every metabolic disease.
completion_criteria.label: Additional variants demonstrate reproducible, timely treatment using the same platform

related_concepts.text: Roster-based conceptual comparison: PED-06, “Prenatal correction that lets severe monogenic disease develop normally,” overlaps in correcting an underlying genetic cause before permanent damage. PED-11 focuses on postnatal prevention of toxic metabolic injury through sufficient hepatic restoration; PED-06 concerns intervention before birth so that development can proceed normally. Their practical boundaries may overlap when metabolic injury begins prenatally, but success after birth would not establish prenatal developmental correction. Only the supplied title and brief comparison were available for PED-06.

Roster-based conceptual comparison: PED-09, “Post-symptomatic restoration of severe genetic neurodevelopmental disorders,” addresses recovery after a phenotype is established. PED-11 aims to prevent metabolic injury before it becomes irreversible. Preserving development through early metabolic control would not demonstrate restoration of established neural circuits. PED-04, “Controlled reopening of developmental critical periods,” likewise concerns a distinct capacity to alter later developmental plasticity; it could become relevant to residual impairment but is not supplied by hepatic editing itself. These comparisons are based on the roster titles rather than reviewed records for those concepts.

Roster-based conceptual comparison: PED-05, “Prevention of cerebral palsy after perinatal brain injury,” shares the goal of preventing lasting childhood disability, but begins from an existing perinatal injury rather than a metabolic defect targeted before irreversible injury. PED-12, “Drug-free donor-specific tolerance for pediatric solid-organ grafts,” shares an interest in reducing lifelong treatment burden. Its mechanism concerns immune acceptance of a graft, whereas PED-11 seeks correction within the child’s own liver cells. These entries remain distinct; their full records were not supplied.

change_log.reason: The evidence supports liver-directed feasibility and a platform goal, while multisystem and brain-restricted disease limit broader extrapolation.

change_log.reason: Editing measurements or surrogate evidence alone do not establish clinical efficacy.

change_log.reason: Those generalizations were not established by the supplied evidence.

change_log.reason: These details materially affect interpretation of feasibility, efficacy, safety and relevance to newborn prevention.

change_log.reason: The original age-or-crisis alternative could admit prior injury, and absence of liver failure alone would miss clinically important harms.

unresolved_issues: The NEJM paper’s exact treatment schedule, seven-week outcomes, publication details and expanded-access designation remain unverified within the supplied review because no source text was retained.
Platform development, trial enrollment and regulatory status as of November 1, 2026 remain unverified; the dated reports do not resolve subsequent progress.
The disease-specific treatment windows, required hepatic functional restoration and manufacturing turnaround needed to prevent irreversible injury are not established here.
Whether a single administration can provide durable benefit, eliminate therapeutic dietary restriction and medication, and preserve development across multiple genes remains to be demonstrated.
The extent to which hepatic correction can prevent neurologic and other extrahepatic complications, particularly in MMA, remains unresolved.
The evidence needed to reuse toxicology across guides, and the extent of regulatory acceptance of such reuse, remain open.

Supplementary material and figure images from the MMA study were not inspected in the supplied review; related-concept comparisons are limited to the supplied roster and brief contextual descriptions.

brief.title: One treatment to stop inherited toxin buildup in babies
possible: A newborn with a severe inherited disorder could receive a single treatment that repairs faulty DNA inside liver cells before toxic substances cause permanent harm. The treatment would restore enough liver function to control the illness as the child grows.

Families could gain lasting freedom from demanding diets and medicines. A shared treatment system would let doctors adapt the approach to additional genes and mutations quickly enough to protect other newborns.
why: An early diagnosis could lead directly to treatment that prevents brain injury and death. For children and their families, lasting disease control would reduce the burden of lifelong care.
Children with rare mutations could benefit from a shared development pathway, rather than needing a separate development effort for every tailored treatment.

sources.showed: This is a report of personalized treatment that edits DNA in an infant with an inherited liver enzyme deficiency.
sources.cited_for: It supports the feasibility of tailoring a treatment to an individual infant.
sources.not_established: It does not establish lasting disease control after a single dose given before permanent injury.

sources.showed: A liver-directed DNA treatment for methylmalonic acidemia, an inherited disorder of food processing, showed signs of gene activity in some children. The trial involving four children ended for lack of benefit, and serious treatment-related reactions occurred.
sources.quote: SUNRISE was terminated due to lack of efﬁcacy.
sources.cited_for: Signs that a treatment has changed liver cells do not establish that it controls the disease.
sources.not_established: This approach did not establish effective, safe disease control or prevention of newborn injury.

sources.who: Kiran Musunuru, Rebecca Ahrens-Niklas and collaborators
sources.showed: An infant received three doses of a tailored DNA treatment and gained partial function in the urea cycle, the body's ammonia disposal system. The team also described plans to extend treatment across related disorders.
sources.quote: Tests demonstrate that he has a partially functional urea cycle.
sources.cited_for: It supports individualized treatment feasibility and describes a planned shared development pathway.
sources.not_established: The case does not establish single-dose prevention of newborn injury or successful reuse across genes.

shown: Musunuru, Ahrens-Niklas and collaborators treated an infant with a tailored DNA repair treatment and reported partial restoration of ammonia disposal. Treatment began at seven months, and the child needed repeated doses.

Bedoyan and colleagues tested a different liver-directed approach in four children with methylmalonic acidemia. It produced signs of gene activity without clinical benefit and caused serious treatment-related reactions. A reusable preventive treatment system remains a goal.
missing: A single treatment has yet to prevent permanent injury and provide lasting disease control across different liver genes.
Treatment must arrive within each disease's prevention window, including diagnosis, design, manufacture and safety review.
Restored liver function must remain sufficient during growth, normal feeding and illness without serious treatment-related harm.
Additional mutations must be treated reproducibly, with an accepted basis for reusing earlier manufacturing and safety work.

milestones.label: Early single-dose treatment succeeds across genes
milestones.explanation: Under a shared protocol, infants treated before injury across different genes would need two years without crises, relevant medicines or restricted protein, while meeting developmental goals. This would establish preventive benefit.

milestones.label: Disease control lasts without serious treatment-related harm
milestones.explanation: Benefit would have to persist through feeding, growth and illness without serious treatment-related harm, with longer monitoring for delayed effects. This would establish control beyond initial improvement.

milestones.label: The same system treats additional mutations in time
milestones.explanation: The same DNA repair tools and delivery particles would need timely, reproducible success across additional mutations, with laboratory support and accepted reuse of safety data. This would establish a reusable treatment system.

uncertain: How early must each disease be treated, and how much liver function must be restored to prevent permanent injury?
How much brain, kidney or heart disease could persist despite successful liver correction?
What evidence would justify sharing safety results across treatments aimed at different mutations?

page.title: Single-dose liver genome editing for neonatal metabolic disease
page.definition: One administration changes DNA in hepatocytes, the liver’s metabolic cells, sufficiently to control a newborn’s inherited metabolic disease and prevent irreversible injury. A shared editing and delivery framework supports treatments for different hepatic metabolic genes, with regulator-accepted reuse of development evidence.

goal.need: Severe CPS1 deficiency has an estimated 50% mortality in early infancy; ammonia crises can cause irreversible neurologic injury before liver transplantation is feasible. MMUT-deficient methylmalonic acidemia can present in the first days to weeks and requires lifelong protein restriction. Liver correction therefore has to arrive within a disease-specific prevention window; in methylmalonic acidemia, it must also be assessed against disease outside the liver.

completion.title: FDA licenses newborn treatments from one liver-editing platform for single-dose prevention across genes.
completion.criterion: FDA licenses products from a shared liver-editing platform for single-administration treatment of newborns with diseases involving different hepatic metabolic genes. Approved indications and supporting clinical evidence establish prevention of irreversible disease-related injury, with disease-specific safety criteria and follow-up. FDA accepts a defined reuse of manufacturing or safety evidence for the additional products. This composite requires preventive clinical benefit and regulatory reuse across genes; it imposes no universal editing fraction, cohort size or follow-up duration.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas; a composite application of FDA licensure and the published platform-development goals.
completion.basis: FDA genome-editing guidance, its February and October 2026 individualized-therapy drafts, THRIVE documents and UCD-101 were searched for a combined single-dose, pre-injury newborn and cross-gene platform test. None specifies one. This Atlas composite uses FDA licensure for each claimed preventive indication and documented regulatory reuse across genes.

milestones.title: A liver-directed editor shows target activity and biological response in preclinical models.
milestones.criterion: Establish feasibility and a scientific rationale through target-cell activity and biological response in relevant preclinical models; FDA specifies no universal editing percentage. In the 2025 CPS1 study, six mice carrying human target sequences, two per dose group, showed up to 42% whole-liver corrective editing; this surrogate model did not establish disease prevention. For MMUT, a 2022 study demonstrated targeted integration and transgene expression in eight mice with humanized livers, four per group, assessed eight weeks after treatment.
milestones.set_by: FDA, Human Gene Therapy Products Incorporating Human Genome Editing, January 2024, section IV; a general genome-editing development criterion.
milestones.threshold_quote: establish feasibility and support the scientific rationale for administration of the investigational human GE product in a clinical trial.

milestones.title: A child receives liver-directed genome editing under an effective IND and ethics approval.
milestones.criterion: A patient receives liver-directed editing after the IND takes effect and ethics approval is obtained. CPS1: one infant received two infusions at approximately 7 and 8 months; the report published on 15 May 2025 recorded no serious adverse events over seven weeks. MMUT: four children aged 20–114 months received single hLB-001 infusions in SUNRISE; enrollment ran from 9 April 2021 to 22 October 2021, with a 23 May 2023 data cutoff. Two developed thrombotic microangiopathy and one cytokine release syndrome.
milestones.set_by: FDA, 21 CFR 312.40 and applicable human-subject protections; CPS1 treatment used single-patient expanded access, whereas SUNRISE was a phase 1/2 clinical investigation.
milestones.threshold_quote: An investigator may not administer an investigational new drug to human subjects until the IND goes into effect under paragraph (b) of this section.

milestones.title: An umbrella IND and clinical trials expand to additional liver-editing products and metabolic diseases.
milestones.criterion: An umbrella IND and associated clinical trials expand to additional editing products and diseases. THRIVE sets this result for genetic medicines generally. CPS1: the UCD-101 sponsor record, last posted on 26 August 2026, lists recruitment and seven planned participants, one infusion and 52 weeks of follow-up. Its umbrella description names seven genes, but displayed molecular eligibility names CPS1; enrollment across genes is not established. MMUT: no corresponding umbrella expansion was identified.
milestones.set_by: ARPA-H, THRIVE award announcement of 9 July 2026; the programme’s expansion criterion is broader than hepatic metabolic disease.
milestones.threshold_quote: teams must demonstrate successful expansion of umbrella investigational new drug application (IND) and clinical trials with additional drug products and diseases

milestones.title: One liver-editing administration produces clinical benefit beyond untreated disease progression.
milestones.criterion: Demonstrate clinical improvement inconsistent with untreated natural history, excluding alternative treatments and natural variability. UCD-101 defines a 16-week response as 100% of age-recommended dietary protein and/or ≥50% less nitrogen-scavenger medication, without associated symptomatic hyperammonemia: ammonia ≥2.5× the upper limit of normal in a non-hemolyzed specimen. This UCD endpoint does not measure neonatal injury prevention. CPS1: the published improvement followed two doses. MMUT: all four SUNRISE participants retained abnormal metabolic measures; the study ended for lack of efficacy.
milestones.set_by: FDA, February 2026 plausible-mechanism draft guidance, section II; nonbinding and not for implementation. The numerical response example is set by sponsor Rebecca Ahrens-Nicklas in UCD-101 and applies to urea-cycle disorders, not methylmalonic acidemia.
milestones.threshold_quote: A substantial improvement in symptoms or change in disease trajectory that is inconsistent with the natural history of the disease

milestones.title: FDA licenses a single-dose liver editor to prevent neonatal injury in one metabolic disease.
milestones.criterion: An approved BLA covers newborn treatment of a hepatic metabolic disease with one administration and prevention of irreversible disease-related injury. The product and manufacturing establishment meet FDA requirements for safety, purity and potency. This applies the general licensing test to the entry’s clinical scope; FDA specifies no universal neonatal efficacy cutoff. Neither k-abe nor hLB-001 appears in FDA’s licensed cellular and gene therapy product list checked on 14 November 2026.
milestones.set_by: FDA, 21 CFR 601.2(a) and (d); the general biologics licensing test is applied here to a single preventive newborn indication.
milestones.threshold_quote: data derived from nonclinical laboratory and clinical studies which demonstrate that the manufactured product meets prescribed requirements of safety, purity, and potency

not_found: No published treatment window, minimum hepatic correction fraction or follow-up duration valid across both disorders was found.
The ClinicalTrials.gov page and API did not expose readable UCD-101 details; the sponsor record was readable through a registry mirror.
UCD-101 lists seven estimated participants but describes five in its brief summary; no reconciliation or posted outcome results was found.
